blocks.heading: The auction you are in
text: Teodora pays the pressing plant and her transaction sits unconfirmed for six hours.
She paid the largest fee in the mempool. Transactions broadcast after hers confirmed while she waited.

blocks.heading: The supply is fixed by rule
text: A block holds at most **4,000,000 weight units** - roughly a million virtual bytes - and one arrives every ten minutes whatever happens.
Demand has no such limit. So this is a fixed supply, sold continuously, and a fee is not a payment. It is a bid.

blocks.heading: And miners are not sentimental
text: They are selling space, so they sort by what each transaction pays **per byte**, not by what it pays in total.
A large generous transaction and a small stingy one are not comparable on the number Teodora was looking at.

blocks.alt: Five transactions sorted by fee rate, with the largest total fee marked as too big and left out while a smaller one gets in
blocks.caption: 14,000 satoshis, left behind. The coffee paying 1,520 confirmed.

blocks.question: Why is Teodora's transaction 1,400 bytes when the coffee's is 190?
answer: Because of lesson 08. Her wallet holds dozens of small outputs, one per record sold, and spending them means naming every one as an input - each with its own signature.
Size is driven by input count, and the fee is charged on bytes rather than on amount. A wallet full of small payments is expensive to spend from, no matter how much it holds.

blocks.heading: The fix has a price attached
text: She should consolidate: sweep the small outputs into one, on a quiet Sunday when rates are low.
Which publishes, in a single transaction, that all forty-one of them share an owner.
Lesson 23 says do not merge your outputs. This lesson says merge them or pay for it forever.
There is no setting that satisfies both. Privacy and fee efficiency are in direct conflict here, and every wallet quietly picks one for you.

blocks.heading: Ethereum's answer to the guessing
text: Under EIP-1559 the protocol sets a **base fee** per unit of gas, adjusts it by up to 12.5% per block to keep blocks about half full, and **burns** it.
You add a tip for the proposer. The base fee is knowable before you send, instead of guessed against an invisible field of rivals.

blocks.heading: But the bid is still public
text: A pending transaction is a statement of exactly what you intend to do, published, before it has happened.
For a payment that is merely a privacy leak. For a trade, it is an invitation.

blocks.title: Sandwiching
text: A bot sees your pending trade, buys ahead of it at a higher fee, lets your trade move the price, and sells into it - all in the same block, all with public information.
The 2019 paper _Flash Boys 2.0_ named and measured this. Nothing was hacked; the mempool did what it is for.

blocks.heading: What she does at 4pm
text: She rebroadcasts with a higher fee. BIP-125 replace-by-fee - the same mechanism that made zero confirmations unsafe in lesson 16 - is here the tool that gets her unstuck.
The transaction confirms in the next block, and the plant ships the test pressings.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: You are not paying a fee, you are bidding in a public auction, and the bid that wins is per byte rather than per payment.
One lesson left in this chapter before the last one. It is about the biggest thefts in the field, none of which touched a chain.
